newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank heralds EMU with two-year policy strategy.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank heralds EMU with two-year policy strategy.

text.p: The German Bundesbank on Thursday paved the way for the switch to a European single currency, mapping out the basis for its policy up until the European Central Bank takes the monetary reins in 1999.

The central bank left interest rates unchanged at its last policy-making meeting of the year, but set a slightly more restrictive target for growth in its main monetary policy indicator, M3 money supply.

In a move aimed at smoothing the transition to Europe's single currency, the central bank said it would extend its money supply orientation to a two-year period, so bridging a possible period of market uncertainty in 1998.

During that year, currencies which enter monetary union will be irrevocably fixed against each other, forcing those central banks affected to coordinate policy very closely until the ECB takes over policy at the start of 1999.
"The two-year orientation is aimed at making the start-up for the European Central Bank as frictionless as possible," Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference.
But he made clear that the new strategy was not a departure from the central bank's fierce anti-inflation stance.
"We want to make clear that we are remaining on a stability path," he said. "That is the clear message of our decisions today and we want to make sure it is understood."

The central bank set a growth target of between 3.5 percent and 6.5 percent for the M3 money supply measure in 1997, slightly lower than the current 4-7 percent range. It watches M3 as a guide to future inflation.

The bank fell short of setting a corridor for 1998 as well -- which some economists had predicted -- but added in a statement that M3 growth of about five percent each year for 1997 and 1998 would be appropriate.

The Bundesbank left the discount rate at 2.50 percent and the Lombard emergency financing rate at 4.50 percent. Its main money market rate, the repo, was held at three percent for the next three weeks, the level which has pertained since August.
Economists polled by Reuters in advance had expected no change in interest rates but had been divided on whether the M3 goal would be kept unchanged or whether it would be lowered.

The Bundesbank compiles its M3 target by looking at likely developments in growth and prices, making adjustments for changes in the way in which money is being used, then placing a target corridor around its central estimate of M3 growth needs.

For 1997, it used an assessment of production potential at just over two percent, unavoidable inflation of between 1.5 and two percent and a one percent element to compensate for slower velocity of circulation of money.
Velocity of circulation is a measure of how intensively funds are used in the economy.

Tietmeyer told a news conference that the two-year M3 money supply growth target was meant to head off any volatility on financial markets that could be disturbed in 1998 in the run-up to a single European currency.
"This is a clear signal of stability for the markets," he said, adding that the M3 money supply measure remained the best indicator for monetary policy.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel welcomed the Bundesbank's decision as a good basis for Europe's single currency.

"With this decision the German Bundesbank underlines its commitment to making a contribution towards creating a stable European currency in a united Europe," Waigel said in a statement released in Bonn.
German industry and most banking groups welcomed the move, although public banks criticised the decision as a "placebo" offered to financial markets rather than a credible policy.
Independent economists saw the decision as a clear statement from the Bundesbank that it wanted the European Central Bank to continue to follow a monetary policy strategy.
